summary: This document describes version 2 of Core Based Trees, a multicast routing protocol that builds one shared distribution tree per group, for use between and within domains. It was published as experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: CBT gives every multicast group one meeting point, called the core. All the routers that carry that group hang off it like branches, and a receiver joins by sending a message towards it.

questions: what is a shared multicast tree
subtitle: Shared-tree multicast routing with one core router per group.

tldr.problem: Multicast routers need to deliver a group's traffic to its receivers, and a source-based tree means separate state for every sender.
tldr.mechanism: CBT version 2 builds one shared tree per group, rooted at a single core router. Routers join by sending JOIN_REQUEST messages towards the core, which are answered with JOIN_ACK; keep-alive ECHO messages check the link to the parent and QUIT and FLUSH messages prune branches that are no longer needed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an Experimental protocol, not an Internet standard, and it is now Historic. Its security considerations section says that security considerations are not addressed in the memo.

sections.title: Core Routers, On-Tree Routers and Upstream
sections.content:
RFC 2189 specifies version 2 of the Core Based Tree (CBT) protocol, a network layer multicast routing protocol that builds a shared multicast distribution tree per group and is suited to inter-domain and intra-domain multicast routing. It may use a separate multicast routing table, or the table of the underlying unicast routing, to establish paths between senders and receivers. The architecture behind it is described in RFC 2201.

The terms are worth stating plainly. A core router is a router that acts as the meeting point between a sender and the group's receivers; the term rendezvous point is used equivalently in some contexts, and a core router need not be configured to know that it is a core. A router that is part of a CBT distribution tree is an on-tree router, and it keeps active state for the group. An upstream interface or router is one that is on the path towards the group's core router, and a downstream one is on the path away from it. The text calls any interface that supports multicast transmission a broadcast interface.

Version 2 differs significantly from version 1 and is not backwards compatible with it, though the authors do not expect extensive compatibility problems because they do not believe CBT was widely deployed at that stage. The main changes are new LAN mechanisms, including the incorporation of a HELLO protocol; new simplified packet formats with a common CBT control packet header; and the rule that each group shared tree has only one active core router. The revision is a complete re-write of the previous one, and any future version of CBT can be expected to be backwards compatible with it.
sections.plainLanguage: CBT gives every multicast group one meeting point, called the core. All the routers that carry that group hang off it like branches, and a receiver joins by sending a message towards it.

sections.title: The Shared Tree and How Data Flows
sections.content:
The protocol is designed to build and maintain a shared multicast distribution tree that spans only those networks and links leading to interested receivers. When a multicast data packet arrives at a router, the router uses the group address as an index into the multicast forwarding cache and forwards a copy of the packet over each interface listed in the entry, except the interface it arrived on.

The state created by a join acknowledgement is bi-directional, so data can flow either way along a branch, and it is group specific: it holds the group address and a list of local interfaces over which join messages for the group have previously been acknowledged. There is no concept of an incoming or an outgoing interface in that state, but the upstream interface still has to be told apart from the downstream ones, and CBT calls them the parent and child interfaces. On link types that do not support native multicast transmission, an on-tree router stores the address of a parent and of any children; on links that support multicast, parent and child information is represented by the local interface addresses over which they are reachable.

Data from a sender that is not a member of the group is encapsulated by the first-hop router using IP-in-IP and unicast to the group's core router, so no group state is required in the network between the first-hop router and the core. At the core router the outer encapsulating header is removed and the packet is disseminated over the group shared tree. All CBT control messages are multicast over multicast supporting links to the all-cbt-routers group, with IP TTL 1, apart from the case where the designated router redirects a join message.
sections.plainLanguage: Data from a member travels down the tree from the core. Data from someone outside the group is wrapped up and sent to the core first, which unwraps it and sends it down. A group needs no state anywhere except on the tree itself.

sections.title: Joining the Tree
sections.content:
A JOIN_REQUEST is the control message that registers a member host's interest in the group's distribution tree, and it can only ever be originated by a leaf router, one with directly attached member hosts. It is sent hop by hop towards the core router for the group. The originating router caches transient state of the form group, incoming interface, outgoing interface, where the outgoing interface is NULL because this router is the originator. That NULL is also what marks the router as responsible for retransmitting the message if no response arrives within the retransmission interval, and it is an error if no response is received after the join timeout. The joining process may then be started again by the next IGMP host membership report from a locally attached host.

A router that is not on-tree, is not the group's core, and has not already forwarded a join for the same group forwards the join to the next hop towards the core and caches the group, the downstream interface it arrived on and the upstream interface it will send it from. Transient state that is never confirmed with a JOIN_ACK times out. When the join reaches the core router, the join is terminated and acknowledged with a JOIN_ACK, and the same happens when it reaches a router that is on-tree over an interface that is not its upstream interface for the group. The JOIN_ACK travels back along the reverse path of the join, which is possible because of the transient state, and once it reaches the router that originated the join the new receiver can receive traffic sent to the group. Receiving a JOIN_ACK creates a forwarding cache entry for the group and marks the upstream interface as the group's parent interface, and the interface the acknowledgement arrived on becomes a child interface.

It cannot be assumed that all the routers on a multi-access link have a uniform view of unicast routing, and that could lead to more than one upstream branch being formed. The routers attached to such a link therefore take part in an explicit election that elects a single router, the designated router, as the link's upstream router for all groups. Since the designated router might not be the link's best next hop for a particular core, a join message may be redirected, in which case the designated router unicasts it across the link to the best next hop, which prevents a looping scenario. This re-direction applies only to join messages, and multicast data never traverses a link more than once.
sections.plainLanguage: A router with a local listener sends a join request towards the core. Each router on the way remembers where the request came from and where it is going. The core, or a router already on the tree, sends an acknowledgement back along the same path, and that is what puts the new receiver on the tree.

sections.title: Leaving the Tree and Detecting Failures
sections.content:
A CBT tree is pruned in the downstream-to-upstream direction whenever a router's child interface list for a group becomes NULL. The router then sends a QUIT_NOTIFICATION to its parent router and deletes all information for that group from its forwarding cache immediately, because a quit is not acknowledged. To reduce the chance of a lost quit leaving the parent with a stale child, a total of MAX_RTX quits are sent, each HOLDTIME seconds after the previous one, and sending the first quit also sends a FLUSH_TREE message over each downstream interface for that group. When a router receives a multicast quit over a parent interface, it schedules a JOIN_REQUEST at a random interval between zero and HOLDTIME seconds, which gives the other routers on the link the opportunity to show that they still want the group before the parent removes the link from its child list.

Each router except the core keeps its upstream link alive by periodically sending an ECHO_REQUEST keepalive to its parent, one message for all the entries that share that parent. On a multicast capable link the keepalive is multicast to the all-cbt-routers group, 224.0.0.15, unless the sending router is the designated router on that interface, in which case it is unicast. The receipt of a keepalive over a valid child interface prompts an ECHO_REPLY, which carries a list of the groups for which the link is a child interface, so that both routers can check that their state agrees. If a group is not refreshed within the group expiry time, a QUIT_NOTIFICATION is sent upstream and a FLUSH_TREE downstream for that group.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers check that the link to the parent is still working by sending a regular hello and waiting for the answer. When a router no longer has anyone downstream who wants the group, it tells its parent it is leaving. When a link fails, the router tells everything below it to stop, so the branch can be rebuilt from scratch.

sections.title: Core Router Discovery
sections.content:
Two options are available. The bootstrap mechanism, as currently specified with the PIM sparse mode protocol, applies only to intra-domain core discovery and allows a plug-and-play type of operation with minimal configuration. Its disadvantage is that it is much more difficult to affect the shape, and thus the optimality, of the resulting distribution tree, and it only applies if every CBT router within the domain implements the bootstrap mechanism. The other option is to configure leaf routers manually with core and group mappings, which imposes administrative burden because the mapping for a particular group has to be coordinated across all leaf routers to ensure consistency and does not scale particularly well. It is likely that better trees result from this method, and it is the only option currently available for inter-domain core discovery.

In the bootstrap mechanism, a subset of the domain's routers is configured to be CBT candidate core routers, and each advertises itself to the domain's Bootstrap Router with a Core Advertisement message. The Bootstrap Router is itself elected dynamically, collects those advertisements, and periodically advertises a candidate core set to the other routers in the domain using Bootstrap Messages. When a router receives an IGMP host membership report from one of its directly attached hosts, it uses a hash function on the reported group address and uses the result as an index into the candidate core set, which is how a local router discovers which core to use for a group. The hash is tailored so that a small number of consecutive groups always hash to the same core, and a bootstrap message can carry a group mask that limits a candidate core set to a particular range of groups, which helps reduce traffic concentration at the core. If the Bootstrap Router detects a core as unreachable, it deletes it from the set it advertises; the local router then re-hashes for each affected group and joins the new core after removing the old state.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have to know which core to join for each group. Either a helper router collects the list of candidate cores and tells everyone, and each router picks one by a fixed rule, or an administrator writes the mapping on every leaf router by hand.

sections.title: The CBT Control Messages
sections.content:
CBT control packets are encapsulated in IP, and IANA has assigned CBT the IP protocol number 7. All CBT control messages have a common fixed length header: a 4-bit version field, which is 2 in this specification, a 4-bit type field, an 8-bit address length giving the length in bytes of the unicast or multicast addresses carried in the packet, and a 16-bit checksum, which is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the entire CBT control packet.

The type field has nine values: 0 HELLO, 1 JOIN_REQUEST, 2 JOIN_ACK, 3 QUIT_NOTIFICATION, 4 ECHO_REQUEST, 5 ECHO_REPLY, 6 FLUSH_TREE, 7 Bootstrap Message and 8 Candidate Core Advertisement, the last two being optional. Each message then adds its own fields. The JOIN_REQUEST carries the group address, the target router that is the core for the group, and the originating router. The JOIN_ACK carries the group address and the target router, which the RFC describes as the router that originated the corresponding JOIN_REQUEST. The QUIT_NOTIFICATION carries the group address and the address of the child router that originates it. The ECHO_REQUEST carries only the address of the originating child router, because group information is not carried in ECHO_REQUEST messages. The ECHO_REPLY carries the address of the originating parent router and the list of group addresses for which that router considers itself a parent over the link in question. The FLUSH_TREE carries the group addresses being flushed, and can specify a single group or all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CBT message starts with the same four-byte header, which says what kind of message it is. After that, each kind of message carries the addresses it needs, such as the group and the routers involved.

fields.desc: Message type, from 0 HELLO to 8 Candidate Core Advertisement.

fields.name: Addr Length

fields.desc: The 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the entire CBT control packet.

items.label: HELLO
items.desc: Used to elect the designated router on a broadcast link.

items.label: JOIN_REQUEST
items.desc: Registers a member host's interest in the group's distribution tree.

items.label: JOIN_ACK
items.desc: Adds an interface to the router's multicast forwarding cache.

items.label: QUIT_NOTIFICATION
items.desc: Tells the parent router that a branch is going away.

items.label: ECHO_REQUEST
items.desc: Keepalive sent by a child router to its parent.

items.label: ECHO_REPLY
items.desc: The parent's answer, listing the groups for which the link is a child interface.

items.label: FLUSH_TREE
items.desc: Tears down all downstream branches for a group.

items.label: Bootstrap Message
items.desc: Optional. Advertises the candidate core set.

items.label: Candidate Core Advertisement
items.desc: Optional. A candidate core announcing itself to the Bootstrap Router.
